 Service Outages in India – CERT-In Rules, Data Protection and Cloud Regulation 
 November 17, 2026 
 Service Outages in India Latest News 
 The global Microsoft 365 outage on November 12-13, which disrupted access to Outlook and other productivity services worldwide, has raised questions about the accountability of cloud service providers and the adequacy of India's regulatory framework for reporting major digital service outages. 
 Background: Microsoft 365 Service Outage 
 An infrastructure-related problem at Microsoft affected customers' ability to access Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook email, across the world.  
 Microsoft attributed the disruption to a fault during an upgrade of its network capacity and issued an apology. 
 The outage also affected services in India. IndiGo and Akasa Air alerted passengers about disruptions to their email support, while Air India rerouted its email services. 
 The incident highlighted India's dependence on cloud-based digital infrastructure and raised an important regulatory question: Are service providers legally required to report technical failures that temporarily disrupt access to essential digital services? 
 India's Regulatory Framework for Service Outages 
 Three major regulatory frameworks are relevant to the reporting and management of digital service disruptions in India. However, each has certain limitations. 
 CERT-In Directions under the Information Technology Act, 2000 
 The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) issued directions on April 28, 2022, under the Information Technology Act, 2000, requiring organisations to report specified cyber incidents within six hours of noticing them. 
 These directions primarily cover cybersecurity incidents such as attacks and intrusions. They do not explicitly include service outages caused by technical faults or infrastructure failures. 
 However, under Section 70B(6) of the IT Act , CERT-In has the authority to call for information and seek explanations from service providers, including Microsoft. 
 Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Directions on IT Outsourcing 
 The RBI's directions on managing risks in outsourcing, issued on November 28, 2025, carry forward the regulatory framework for outsourced IT services that initially took effect on October 1, 2023. 
 Under these directions, banks procuring cloud services must assess their dependence on service providers and maintain an appropriate exit strategy. 
 If an outsourced arrangement fails, the RBI can hold the bank accountable for ensuring continuity and managing associated risks. The bank may also seek an explanation from the cloud service provider under its contractual agreement. 
 Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 
 The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023, introduces another dimension to the regulation of service outages. 
 The Act defines a personal data breach to include the accidental loss of access to personal data. Under the Rules scheduled to come into effect in May 2027, personal data breaches must be reported to the Data Protection Board and the affected individuals. 
 Failure to report a breach could attract a penalty of up to Rs. 200 crore . 
 However, the framework creates an important ambiguity: it is unclear whether a temporary service outage constitutes a legally reportable loss of access to personal data. 
 International Frameworks for Cloud Service Accountability 
 Several countries have established more direct regulatory mechanisms to monitor major digital service providers. 
 European Union 
 The European Union has introduced regulatory oversight of critical technology providers through two important frameworks. 
 Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA): The EU's financial supervisors identified 19 critical technology service providers under DORA on November 18, 2025. The framework places major technology vendors providing services to financial institutions under the supervision of European financial regulators. 
 Network and Information Security Directive 2 (NIS2): Unlike DORA, NIS2 covers cloud service providers across sectors. Cloud service providers must notify the national authority within 24 hours and submit a detailed notification within 72 hours. 
 United Kingdom 
 As of July 13, 2026, the United Kingdom had placed Microsoft and three other technology companies under the oversight of the Bank of England. 
 This framework, like DORA, focuses on technology services supplied to financial institutions. 
 Singapore 
 On October 7, Singapore passed a digital infrastructure law requiring large data centres and cloud service providers to obtain licences and report service interruptions to the regulator. 
 South Korea 
 Following a data centre fire in October 2022 that disrupted the messaging platform KakaoTalk, South Korea introduced stronger disaster-management requirements.  
 Since July 2023, large digital platforms and data centres have been required to submit disaster management plans to the government. 
 Options Available to Indian Customers 
 At present, a customer's primary recourse against a cloud service provider is generally governed by the contractual agreement.  
 If the provider fails to meet the agreed service-level requirements, the customer may be entitled to service credits, which provide a discount on a future bill. 
 The regulatory framework could be strengthened through four possible measures: 
 Expand CERT-In reporting requirements: Major service disruptions should be reportable irrespective of whether they result from cyberattacks, technical faults or infrastructure failures. 
 Direct regulatory oversight: The government could bring the largest digital service providers under the supervision of a designated regulator. 
 Clarify data breach obligations: The Data Protection Board could clarify whether temporary outages constitute personal data breaches under the DPDP framework and identify the entities responsible for reporting them before the Rules take effect in May 2027. 
 Diversify service providers: Government organisations could reduce dependence on foreign cloud service providers by using domestic alternatives. In December 2025, the Union Government informed the Lok Sabha that 12.68 lakh official email accounts had shifted to a platform operated by Chennai-based Zoho. However, domestic providers would also need clear outage-reporting obligations. 
 Source: TH 
 Service Outages in India FAQs
 Q1: What is CERT-In?
 Ans: The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team is the national agency responsible for responding to cybersecurity incidents and coordinating cyber incident reporting under the Information Technology Act, 2000.
 Q2: What is the reporting timeline under CERT-In's 2022 directions?
 Ans: Organisations are required to report specified cybersecurity incidents within six hours of noticing them.
 Q3: Why does the DPDP Act matter in the context of service outages?
 Ans: The Act includes accidental loss of access to personal data within its definition of a personal data breach. This raises questions about whether temporary service outages trigger reporting obligations.
 Q4: What is the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA)?
 Ans: DORA is an EU regulatory framework that strengthens the digital operational resilience of financial entities and brings critical technology service providers under regulatory oversight.
 Q5: How does the EU's NIS2 framework regulate cloud outages?
 Ans: It defines significant incidents using outage-duration and user-impact thresholds and requires notification within 24 hours, followed by a detailed report within 72 hours.
 RERA Reforms for Homebuyers: Five Changes Needed After a Decade 
 November 17, 2026 
 RERA Reforms for Homebuyers Latest News 
 A decade after the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 (RERA) was passed, a homebuyers’ body wrote to PM Modi (in October 2026), arguing the law had failed to fulfil its objectives.  
 Cabinet Secretary T.V. Somanathan acknowledged the concerns recently, and officials subsequently met the forum’s representatives— signalling the matter is being taken up at the highest levels of government.  
 The episode highlights persistent implementation gaps in one of India’s key consumer-protection laws. 
 What Is RERA and Why It Matters 
 Enacted in 2016 , RERA established a Real Estate Regulatory Authority (RERA) in each state, along with a national-level Central Advisory Council. 
 Twin objectives: Protect homebuyers’ interests (especially against delayed projects and broken builder promises) while also promoting the real estate sector. 
 The petitioning body — Forum for People’s Collective Efforts (FPCE) — had itself been instrumental in the original campaign to pass RERA, making its current criticism particularly significant. 
 Key Reform #1: Shift Oversight to Consumer Affairs 
 Currently, RERA falls under the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA). 
 FPCE’s suggestion: Split the dual mandate —  
 Sector promotion should remain with MoHUA. 
 Homebuyer protection should move to the Department of Consumer Affairs. 
 Rationale: A single ministry simultaneously promoting the industry and protecting consumers creates an inherent conflict of interest. 
 Key Reform #2: Create a National Appellate Tribunal for Real Estate 
 Currently, appeals go to State Appellate Tribunals, leading to inconsistent interpretation of the same central law across states. 
 FPCE’s proposal : Establish a National Appellate Tribunal for Real Estate, modelled on the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) and National Green Tribunal (NGT). 
 Why this matters: “A homebuyer’s rights depend on where he happened to buy” — a single national appellate body would create uniform RERA jurisprudence across India. 
 Current institutional gaps : Several states have had no Chairperson or Members appointed to their tribunals; one state tribunal even lacked quorum to pass any order at all. 
 Key Reform #3: Make the Agreement for Sale (AFS) Part of the Act Itself 
 At present, the Agreement for Sale (AFS) — the core contract between buyer and builder — is governed only by Rules under the Act, not the Act itself. 
 FPCE’s concern : This makes the AFS easy to dilute, since builders can deviate from the model agreement. 
 Proposed fix : Include the AFS in a Schedule to the Act, making it a binding statutory document. 
 Notably, the Ministry Secretary himself flagged concern in January 2024 over “the very relevance of having a model AFS when builders are deviating from it” — reinforcing that a non-binding model offers no real protection. 
 Key Reform #4: Statutory Exit Option for Buyers in Personal Distress 
 Section 18 of the Act currently provides an exit route only when the developer is at fault (e.g., project delays). 
 Gap identified: No provision exists for buyers needing to exit due to personal circumstances — job loss, death of an earning family member, etc. 
 FPCE’s analogy: “A developer in distress may approach the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT); a family in distress has nowhere to go.” 
 Specific Proposal :  
 Cancellation within one year of booking → full refund within one month. 
 Cancellation after one year → full refund plus interest at the SBI savings account rate, with no questions asked. 
 Key Reform #5: Automatic Compensation for All Allottees 
 Current system flaw : Compensation is paid only to homebuyers who file complaints and pursue lengthy legal battles — and “the overwhelming majority never do.” 
 This allows builders to treat compensation as a “modest and predictable cost of business,” effectively pricing in non-compliance in advance. 
 FPCE’s proposal : Make compensation automatic for every allottee when a project is delayed or deficient — without requiring individual complaints. 
 Mechanism suggested : The promoter must submit a complete list of allottees to RERA, which should then proactively contact all of them to collect bank details for disbursement. 
 Conclusion 
 A decade on, RERA’s promise of robust homebuyer protection remains only partially realised — hampered by fragmented state-level enforcement, a dilutable model agreement, and compensation mechanisms that favour inaction by builders.  
 The proposed reforms — institutional restructuring, statutory safeguards, and automatic compensation — offer a roadmap to transform RERA from a well-intentioned law into an effectively enforced one. 
 Source: IE 
 RERA reforms for homebuyers FAQs
 Q1: Why are RERA reforms for homebuyers being demanded after a decade? 
 Ans: RERA reforms for homebuyers are sought because fragmented enforcement, delayed justice and weak compensation mechanisms have prevented the 2016 law from fully protecting buyers.
 Q2: Why has the proposed reform suggested shifting homebuyer protection to Consumer Affairs? 
 Ans: RERA reforms for homebuyers propose shifting consumer protection to the Department of Consumer Affairs, separating it from MoHUA’s responsibility for promoting the real estate sector.
 Q3: How would a National Appellate Tribunal strengthen RERA enforcement? 
 Ans: RERA reforms for homebuyers propose a national appellate tribunal to ensure consistent interpretation of the law and reduce differences across state-level tribunals.
 Q4: Why should the Agreement for Sale become part of the RERA Act? 
 Ans: RERA reforms for homebuyers seek statutory recognition of the Agreement for Sale, preventing builders from diluting contractual safeguards through deviations from model agreements.
 Q5: What changes are proposed regarding buyer exits and compensation? 
 Ans: RERA reforms for homebuyers propose statutory exit options for buyers facing personal distress and automatic compensation for allottees affected by delayed or deficient projects.
 PLI Scheme: Strong Investment Growth but Employment Generation Lags 
 November 17, 2026 
 PLI Scheme Latest News 
 A joint NITI Aayog-IIM Ahmedabad impact assessment report, released recently, evaluated the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme — one of the Modi government’s flagship manufacturing initiatives, launched in March 2020.  
 Six years on, the report reveals a mixed picture: strong progress on investment and production, but significant lag in employment generation — raising important questions about the scheme’s design and effectiveness. 
 What Is the PLI Scheme? 
 Introduced in 2020, following the 2019 corporate tax rate cuts, to encourage entrepreneurs to build new manufacturing capacity in India. 
 Core design principle : Unlike broad-based or untargeted subsidies, PLI links government incentives directly to incremental production and performance by firms. 
 Dual objective : Catalyse investment and enhance firm-level competitiveness. 
 Covers 14 schemes across key sectors, with a total outlay of ₹1.91 lakh crore. 
 Manufacturing growth remains a policy priority, given its potential to provide meaningful employment to India’s large, young, expanding workforce. 
 Headline Numbers: Investment and Production vs Employment 
 Investment: Achieved 76% of target, cumulatively attracting ₹2.40 lakh crore. 
 Production: Achieved 64% of target, generating ₹22.66 lakh crore worth of output. 
 Employment: Only 28% of target achieved — just 8.49 lakh jobs created against a target of 30.18 lakh jobs. 
 This stark gap between investment/production progress and employment outcomes is the report’s central concern. 
 Sector-wise Employment Performance: Wide Variations 
 Top Job Creators: 
 Food products PLI: 3.29 lakh jobs (highest) 
 Large-scale electronics manufacturing: 1.69 lakh jobs 
 Pharma drugs manufacturing: 1.14 lakh jobs 
 Below-Target Performers: 
 Automobiles and auto components: 67,820 jobs (against a target of 1.48 lakh — less than half) 
 White goods: 52,703 jobs 
 Telecom and networking: 33,610 jobs 
 Textiles: 33,427 jobs 
 Solar PV modules, speciality steel, bulk drugs, medical devices, IT hardware, drones/drone components, battery manufacturing: each below 15,000 jobs 
 Sectors “broadly on track ” (as per the report): Large-scale electronics, pharmaceuticals, food processing, drones, medical devices, and white goods showed strong progress across multiple parameters (investment, production, employment, exports). 
 Sectors needing strengthening : Automobiles and auto components, telecom, and speciality steel require further work on employment, exports, and domestic value addition. 
 Why the Employment Lag? Understanding Gestation Periods 
 Manufacturing investments follow a sequential pattern : investment happens first → production ramps up as capacity is commissioned → employment grows only as operations reach commercial scale. 
 This means investment, production, and employment need not progress at the same pace — a natural lag exists . 
 Implementation status : The 14 schemes have completed 58% of their aggregate implementation period (578 of 996 months) — meaning 42% of the implementation period remains, so final judgment on full-tenure targets would be premature. 
 Why Are Targets Not Being Met? Structural Issues 
 Stringent targets, especially in sectors with long gestation periods and high demand uncertainty (due to international trade dynamics and geopolitical shifts), discourage scheme adoption. 
 Industrial mechanisation can also make it harder for sectors to meet employment targets even as production rises. 
 The report stresses: industry participation in designing sector-specific targets is essential for better outcomes. 
 PLI, in its current form, is a purely supply-side scheme — the report recommends adding demand-side support, i.e., incentivising downstream firms and consumers to purchase from PLI-supported firms. 
 Disbursement Lag: Money Not Fully Flowing 
 Cumulative incentive disbursements stood at just 18.51% of the total ₹1.91 lakh crore outlay (as of March 2026). 
 9 of 14 schemes — including bulk drugs, automobiles, and textiles — had disbursements below 10% of their allocated outlay. 
 In contrast, drones, large-scale electronics, and food products schemes saw disbursements of 25-77% of outlay — reflecting their more mature implementation stage. 
 Capital-intensive sectors may show strong investment without proportionate employment growth; technology-intensive sectors often need longer gestation periods before production and export outcomes materialise. 
 The Bigger Picture: A Scheme of Varying Objectives 
 The report highlights that PLI schemes are not uniform in objectives or implementation trajectory:  
 Some sectors prioritise building domestic capacity and reducing import dependence. 
 Others focus on achieving scale, boosting exports, and securing positions in global value chains. 
 Despite employment shortfalls, nearly 70% of targeted segments remain broadly on track, underscoring PLI’s overall positive role in India’s manufacturing push. 
 Way Forward: Key Recommendations 
 Adopt a more sector-specific approach, given wide variation in performance across sectors. 
 Standardise data collection and reporting mechanisms across different ministries implementing PLI schemes. 
 Move beyond supply-side intervention — incorporate demand-side incentives for downstream firms and consumers to buy from PLI-supported companies. 
 Conclusion 
 Six years in, the PLI scheme has proven its worth in driving investment and production, but its employment promise remains only partially fulfilled.  
 Bridging this gap will require sector-specific calibration, demand-side support, and patience — recognising that manufacturing employment, unlike capital inflows, takes longer to mature into tangible jobs for India’s workforce. 
 Source: IE | IE 
 PLI Scheme FAQs
 Q1: What is the objective of the PLI scheme? 
 Ans: The PLI scheme was launched in 2020 to encourage manufacturing capacity by linking government incentives to firms’ incremental production and performance across 14 sectors.
 Q2: How has the PLI scheme performed in investment, production and employment generation? 
 Ans: The PLI scheme achieved 76% of its investment target and 64% of production target, but created only 8.49 lakh jobs against 30.18 lakh targeted.
 Q3: Which sectors have generated the most employment under the PLI scheme? 
 Ans: The PLI scheme generated the most jobs in food products, with 3.29 lakh, followed by large-scale electronics manufacturing and pharmaceutical drugs.
 Q4: Why has employment generation under the PLI scheme lagged behind investment and production? 
 Ans: The PLI scheme faces employment lags due to manufacturing gestation periods, stringent targets, industrial mechanisation and uncertainty surrounding international demand and trade.
 Q5: What reforms does the impact assessment recommend for the PLI scheme? 
 Ans: The PLI scheme needs sector-specific targets, standardised data reporting and demand-side incentives encouraging downstream firms and consumers to purchase from supported manufacturers.
